newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RESULTS TODAY - SAMANCOR YR SHARE SEEN DOWN.
newsitem.headline: RESULTS TODAY - SAMANCOR YR SHARE SEEN DOWN.

text.p: South African metals firm Samancor Ltd, the world's biggest producer of ferro-chrome, is set to post a steep drop in year profit as price falls buffet its key markets, analysts said.
The firm is exposed to highly cyclical metals markets which have come off peaks seen last year as both chrome and manganese prices slipped.
The deteriorating market conditions saw Samancor issue a profit warning in April and revise its forecasts for the second half.

The firm had initially plumped for second half numbers broadly similar to those seen in the first half, but it said a strenghtening rand, lower than expected managanese prices and production problems at its Metalloy division would all now hit the figures.
"Chrome prices have been lower, but manganese prices have been unexpectedly lower," said Albert Minassian, analyst at HSBC Simpson McKie.

Analysts' forecasts for pre-exceptional earnings per share were on a range of 120 cents to 172, against 355 cents last time. The dividend was seen being slashed from 170 cents to a range of 50 cents to 80.
The consensus figures were for earnings of 142 cents a share and a shareholder payout of 67 cents.

However, analysts noted the group had sold its 50 percent stake in graphite electrode maker EMSA to joint-venture partner UCAR International for 335 million rand. The cash from the deal will see attributable profit actually rise over last year.

Analysts were split on the prospects for ferrochrome prices in the current year, with some expecting them to continue a recent rally, while others were already seeing pressure coming back in and knocking prices back.
The chrome market has been soaking up increased capacity from Chromecorp Holdings Ltd and also a revitalised chrome industry in Kazakhstan.
However, most analysts agreed the firm would probably bounce its earnings from this low point as it goes forward, possibly topping 400 cents a share in 1999.

Problems that have beset the firm's interest in its Columbus Steel joint-venture also look to be on the mend. Losses at the project are still going to impact heavily on the results being published Monday, but analysts said Columbus was starting to improve.
"Columbus seems to be turning the corner," said George Grohmann, analyst at Rice, Rinaldi, Turner.
Samancor owns 33 percent of Columbus, with the remainder split between Highveld Steel & Vanadium and state-owned Industrial Development Corp.
The project, one of the world's biggest stainless steel producers, has been beset by commissioning problems, but Highveld said on Monday that Columbus' losses were narrowing.

"Columbus' operations have improved and its markets are capable of absorbing the additional materials as production levels increase gradually towards full capacity," managing director Trevor Jones said at news conference with the firm's half year results.
